output:
*Interview with Odile Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Madame, thank you for waiting. I know you have had a dreadful time. I shall ask only what I need. Will you tell me about dinner?

MME MONNIER: There is little pleasant to tell, Monsieur l'Inspecteur, but I will tell it in order. My husband has done the same thing every New Year's Eve. When the temple struck nine, he made everyone at table show their watches. He liked to be right about other people's time. Félix's watch showed twenty minutes to nine. Aurèle scolded him for it. Félix made a joke of it, as he does when he is frightened.

MATTHEY: Did your husband say anything about the watch itself?

MME MONNIER: He said it was a sentimental object and not a useful one, which is what he always said about his brother's silver watch. Félix has never let anyone touch it, not even his uncle. I do not know why he carries it.

MATTHEY: And Monsieur Girard?

MME MONNIER: He and my husband quarrelled about the price of the repeater. Monsieur Girard wished to buy the rights to it, and Aurèle would not take what he was offered. It was an unpleasant quarrel, but Monsieur Girard is a blunt man and says what he thinks about money. My husband respected that, though he did not enjoy losing.

MATTHEY: After dinner, what did you do?

MME MONNIER: Casimir and I played piquet in the salon. We have played together a great many times, and he is the oldest friend in this house. We did not stop for a break. The temple struck ten while we were playing. We went on playing until he went out to fetch his cigars. He is never without them between hands.

MATTHEY: Did you notice the time when he went out?

MME MONNIER: I did not look at the clock when he went. I was looking at my cards, as one does at piquet. I do not look at clocks in this house. I have never needed to.

MATTHEY: Before he left, did he say anything to you?

MME MONNIER: He asked me to play for him. I sat down at the piano at once and played Chopin, because it is what he liked best from me. I played until he came back, and I stopped when he came in.

MATTHEY: When he came back, what happened?

MME MONNIER: A moment after he came back, the hall clock struck eleven. I remember it because it struck, and because I was thinking that Casimir would want his cigar and would be cross that it had gone out.

MATTHEY: Madame, I must ask about your husband.

MME MONNIER: I have nothing to add to what I told the constables. Aurèle was a difficult man and a very good watchmaker, and I was his wife. I know that is what you expect me to say, and I shall not say more than that. I will not weep for you, Monsieur, and I would ask you not to expect it.

MATTHEY: Is there anything about Félix you think I should know?

MME MONNIER: Félix owes money. I know this because Aurèle told me, and some of what he owes is owed to Monsieur Girard. Félix is young and charming and he has always been careless with both. That is not a crime, though my husband did not think it a virtue either.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Madame. That is all for now.

MME MONNIER: You are very kind, Monsieur l'Inspecteur. I hope you will be quick. The doctor will want to go home, and so, I think, will Félix.
